relationship_to_restored_text: Interpretive contemplative layer aligned by verse. This does not replace the source-audited restored translation.

verses.mystical_translation: Solomon gathers women from many peoples into the orbit of one royal household.
The narrative fears religious turning through intimate foreign ties, yet the greater power belongs to the king who accumulates them.
One thousand wives and concubines reveal not romance but an empire expressed through women's bodies.
In old age Solomon's heart is divided, but age itself is not the sin.
He participates in the worship of neighboring peoples.
The wise king is judged for incomplete faithfulness.
He builds high places near Jerusalem for Moabite and Ammonite worship.
The court's many religious communities receive royal sanctuaries.
The problem is framed as Solomon's turned heart after repeated encounters with YHWH.
Knowledge and command did not guarantee practice.
The kingdom that Solomon centralized will be torn from his house.
The rupture is delayed into his son's generation for David's sake.
A remnant of dynasty and Jerusalem is preserved.
Hadad the Edomite rises as an adversary with a story older than Solomon's failure.
David's war in Edom and Joab's killing campaign stand behind his resistance.
Six months of killing every male reveal the massacre beneath imperial peace.
Hadad escapes as a small child with surviving Edomites.
Egypt gives the refugees house, food, and land.
Hadad is drawn into Pharaoh's family through marriage.
His son grows within the royal household of asylum.
When David and Joab are dead, Hadad asks to return home.
Material safety has not erased his longing for land and people.
Rezon also rises from the wreckage of David's wars.
A band of displaced fighters becomes a government in Damascus.
Solomon's reign faces resistance from peoples the Davidic empire harmed.
Jeroboam, son of a named widow, lifts his hand from within Solomon's own administration.
The revolt grows beside royal construction and repair.
Solomon promotes Jeroboam because he is capable, placing him over forced labor.
A prophet meets the labor official alone outside Jerusalem.
A new garment is torn before the kingdom itself tears.
Ten pieces become a promise of ten tribes.
One portion remains with David's house and Jerusalem.
The oracle judges the court's divided worship, though the women and foreign peoples must not carry Solomon's responsibility.
Solomon remains in office because of the idealized memory of David.
The next generation will bear the political rupture.
A lamp remains in Jerusalem as a sign of continuity without total possession.
Jeroboam is offered the kingdom his desire reaches toward.
His dynasty, too, is made conditional upon listening and justice.
David's house will be humbled but not erased forever.
Solomon responds to prophetic succession by trying to kill the rival, and Egypt shelters another fugitive.
The official record closes over acts and wisdom not preserved here.
Forty years of reign reach their end.
Solomon is buried, and Rehoboam inherits a kingdom already cracking.

contemplative_note: The chapter is often read as foreign women ruining a wise man. A more honest reading sees a king who accumulated women, labor, wealth, and conquered peoples until the survivors of imperial violence and the workers inside his system became agents of rupture.
